title: Dhul-Jalali wal-Ikram
tomorrow: what's fair when the one who wronged you is thirteen?

lines: WIN THE MOMENT, LOSE THE PERSON?
cards: A kid at a counter, hands jammed in his hoodie pocket, saying sorry to an adult while his mom waits by the door. Maybe you've stood on one side of a moment like that. Maybe both.
Yesterday's question: when the apology finally comes, how do you take it without making the other person smaller? You can win the moment. You can also lose the person.
The Qur'an has a two-part Name that holds exactly that balance.

teach.b: In Surah ar-Rahman, after a long list of gifts, the verses turn: "Everyone that is thereon will pass away; There remaineth but the Countenance of thy Lord of Might and Glory."
In Arabic, that title is Dhul-Jalali wal-Ikram.

Jalal is majesty, greatness that doesn't need anyone's applause. Ikram is honoring, generosity, treating someone as worth something. Put together, it's a greatness that gives dignity instead of taking it.
Nothing about that majesty requires anyone to be made small. Here's a line to tell a friend tonight.
The Prophet, peace be upon him, used this Name in the words he said right after finishing a prayer: Allahumma antas-salam wa minkas-salam, tabarakta ya dhal-jalali wal-ikram.

You are Peace, and from You is peace; blessed are You, Lord of Majesty and Generosity. And in another report, he told people to hold fast to ya dhal-jalali wal-ikram when they call on God. So back to the counter.

teach.h: YOU DON'T NEED TO WIN. HONOR HIM.
teach.b: Jalal says: you don't need to win this.
Ikram says: honor him for coming. The two together might look like naming what happened plainly, thanking him for saying it, and pulling out a chair.

how: After prayer, Muslims say the Prophet's words: Allahumma antas-salam wa minkas-salam, tabarakta ya dhal-jalali wal-ikram.

o: Lord of the Heavens and Earth

games.q: a two-part Name — tap the pairs.
p: the Countenance of thy Lord remains

s: this Name comes from Surah ar-Rahman
"There remaineth but the Countenance of thy Lord of Might and Glory."
ikram is just another word for God's power
ikram is honoring and generosity: greatness that gives others dignity.
the Prophet used this Name in the words he said right after a prayer
tabarakta ya dhal-jalali wal-ikram: blessed are You, Lord of Majesty and Generosity.

games.q: a teammate who mocked you all season apologizes at practice, in front of everyone. what fits today's Name?
o: accept it plainly, thank them for saying it, and let them keep their dignity.
have them spell out every single thing they did, so it really counts.
laugh and say it never bothered you, so nobody feels awkward.
games.why: jalal: you don't need to win. ikram: honor the one who came. the second option wins the moment; the third hides the truth.

practice: Say the phrase slowly, out loud or under your breath: ya dhal-jalali wal-ikram, O Lord of Majesty and Generosity. Between each saying, bring to mind one person it would cost you something to honor this week.
Let the phrase and that face sit side by side until the bell.

wordCard.voice: Dhul-Jalali wal-Ikram. Lord of Majesty and Generosity: great enough that no one needs to be made small.

orig.note: Arabic: Lord of Majesty and Generosity, from Surah ar-Rahman.

carryVoice: Here's the line: majesty and honor, with room at the counter for both people. Until tomorrow.
